response.answer: The model-X knockoff generator handles mixed predictor types by fitting separate conditional models for each type. Swap diagnostics and thresholds indicate failure when they do not match the original model's behavior.

results.title: Should I Specify a Model Predictor Variable as Categorical or Continuous? - The Analysis Factor
results.content: # Should I Specify a Model Predictor Variable as Categorical or Continuous? Predictor variables in statistical models can be treated as either continuous or categorical. Likewise, continuous predictors, like age, systolic blood pressure, or percentage of ground cover should be specified as continuous. But there are numerical predictors that aren’t continuous. Count predictor variables, like number of therapy sessions or number of symptoms, are numerical but not continuous. This also happens in data sets where a potentially continuous variable has few values in the data set, intentionally or not. If you specify a predictor as continuous, the software will fit a best-fitting regression line between that predictor and Y, the response variable, after accounting for other variables in the model. Because a discrete predictor *is* numerical, fitting a line to it can be reasonable. If you specify a predictor as categorical, the software will estimate a mean of Y for each category of the predictor (shown below in red). You need a minimum of 3 values of X to fit a line, but with only 3, it can be hard to tell if there really is a linear trend. The more values of X, the more cumbersome it is to have a set of mean differences and the more clearly you can fit a line (or a curve). results.content: Using the error-model specification, we can think of any measurement of \(Y\) as an expected value plus some random value sampled from a normal distribution with a specified variance. Because it is \(Y\) and not some “error” that is drawn from the specified distribution, I refer to this as the **conditional-draw** specification of the linear model. The error-draw specification “generates” data by 1) constructing what \(y\_i\) “should be” given \(x\_i\) (this is the conditional expection), then 2) adding some error \(e\_i\) drawn from a normal distribution with mean zero and some specified variance. The error-draw specification is not very useful for thinking about data generation for data analyzed by generalized linear models, which are models that allow one to specify distribution families other than Normal (such as the binomial, Poisson, and Gamma families). Unlike the error and conditional draw specifications above, the ANOVA model doesn’t have a linear predictor in the form of a regression equation (or the equation for a line) – that is, there are neither \(X\) variables nor coefficients (\(\beta\)). ## 8.2 A linear model can be fit to data with continuous, discrete, or categorical \(X\) variables. In the linear model fit to the data in Figure 8.1B, the \(X\) variable is **continuous**, which can take any real number between the minimum \(X\) and maximum \(X\) in the data. ### 8.2.1 Fitting linear models to experimental data in which the \(X\) variable is continuous or discrete. A linear model fit to data with a numeric (continous or discrete) \(X\) is classical **regression** and the result is typically communicated by a regression line. ### 8.2.2 Fitting linear models to experimental data in which the \(X\) variable is categorical. Linear models can be fit to experimental data in which the \(X\) variable is categorical – this is the focus of this text! Perhaps surprisingly, 1) we can fit a model like equation (8.2) to data in which the \(X\) variable is categorical and 2) the coefficient of \(X\) *is* a slope. * **independent variables** (often shortened to IV) – “independent” in the sense that in a statistical model at least, the \(X\) are not a function of \(Y\).

results.title: Regression Analysis | Examples of Regression Models | Statgraphics
results.content: Regression analysis is used to model the relationship between a response variable and one or more predictor variables. STATGRAPHICS Centurion provides a large number of procedures for fitting different types of regression models:. The simplest regression models involve a single response variable Y and a single predictor variable X. The Multiple Regression procedure fits a model relating a response variable Y to multiple predictor variables X1, X2, ... STATGRAPHICS will fit parallel or non-parallel linear regressions for each level of a "BY" variable and perform statistical tests to determine whether the intercepts and/or slopes of the lines are significantly different. In STATGRAPHICS, the Regression Model Selection procedure implements such a scheme, selecting the models which give the best values of the adjusted R-Squared or of Mallows' Cp statistic. More: Regression Model Selection.pdf. Most least squares regression programs are designed to fit models that are linear in the coefficients. To describe the impact of external variables on failure times, regression models may be fit. For this reason, STATGRAPHICS provides a special procedure that will fit life data regression models with censoring, assuming either an exponential, extreme value, logistic, loglogistic, lognormal, normal or Weibull distribution. For response variables that are counts, STATGRAPHICS provides two procedures: a Poisson Regression and a Negative Binomial Regression. The Orthogonal Regression procedure is designed to construct a statistical model describing the impact of a single quantitative factor X on a dependent variable Y, when both X and Y are observed with error. 1. *Regression models* that predict the value of a dependent variable. The *Piecewise Linear Regression* procedure is designed to fit a regression model where the relationship between the dependent variable Y and the independent variable X is a continuous function consisting of 2 or more linear segments. The *Quantile Regression* procedure fits linear models to describe the relationship between selected quantiles of a dependent variable Y and one or more independent variables. The *Zero Inflated Count Regression* procedure is designed to fit a regression model in which the dependent variable *Y* consists of counts. The fitted regression model relates *Y* to one or more predictor variables *X*, which may be either quantitative or categorical.

results.title: Under what circumstances should we categorize continuous predictors in regression models? | ResearchGate
results.content: # Under what circumstances should we categorize continuous predictors in regression models? I can't find a definite answer in web that why some studies categorize age in regression models to find out significant factors associated with a response variable. One situation in which we need categorizing continuous data is handling **inapplicable** features. Categorizing a continuous independent variable has many consequences: loss of information and statistical power, underestimate the variance, residual confounding, obscure the non-linearity, etc. If you have lots of observations, you MAY ALSO try out some categorization of x and use a set of dummy variables (and a reference value) to highlight the non-linearity in the most efficient way. One can categorize the continuous predictors in regression models if it will give a better understanding of relationship among variables especially when dealing with age related issues. As a rule of thumb I think using continuous data for modeling and using categorization to explore or describe the behavior of a model (e.g., graphically) can be a good combination. If a researcher is interested in the effects of each level of a categorised predictor on the dependent variable, He/she has no alternative than to categorise the predictor variable even though information will be lost. Generally, it is advisable to leave the predictor variable (e.g. age) as continuous when carrying out regression model to avoid loss of information unless the research interest lies on the effects of the levels of the categorised predictor variable. Actually, Thom Baguley 's answer made me recall one very useful application of categorising a continuous variable. b) When there are few values of the continues variable or a non-linear relationship (as mentioned by Christer Thrane Thom Baguley ). An example of trial and error to find the best model is categorization. Regression model for continuous dependent variable and multiple ordinal predictors?
